title: Google SRE Book, Chapter 4: Service Level Objectives (Betsy Beyer et al.)
text:
## SLI, SLO, SLA definitions

A Service Level Indicator (SLI) is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service that is provided. Common SLIs include request latency, error rate, system throughput, availability, and durability. A Service Level Objective (SLO) is a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by an SLI, typically structured as SLI less than or equal to target, or lower bound less than or equal to SLI less than or equal to upper bound. A Service Level Agreement (SLA) is an explicit or implicit contract with your users that includes consequences of meeting (or missing) the SLOs it contains. The distinguishing feature: if there are no explicit consequences for missing the targets, you are looking at an SLO, not an SLA.

## Categories of indicator

Different classes of service care about different indicators. User facing serving systems generally care about availability, latency, and throughput: can we respond to the request, how long did it take, and how many requests can be handled. Storage systems emphasize latency, availability, and durability: how long to read or write, can we access the data on demand, and is the data still there when we need it. Big data systems such as data processing pipelines care about throughput and end to end latency. Correctness is an attribute of interest for every system.

## Aggregation and percentiles

Most metrics are better thought of as distributions rather than averages. Averaging request latencies may seem attractive but obscures tail behavior: a small number of very slow requests can matter more than the mean. Using high order percentiles such as the 50th, 95th, 99th, and 99.9th reveals the long tail and the worst case that a fraction of users actually experience. The higher the variance in response times, the more the typical user experience is affected by the tail.

## Choosing targets

Five recommendations for choosing SLO targets: do not pick a target based on current performance, because current performance may require heroic effort to sustain; keep it simple, since complicated aggregations obscure changes; avoid absolutes such as infinitely scalable or always available; have as few SLOs as possible, just enough for good coverage; and do not make the SLO too tight too early, start loose and refine over time as you learn.

## Error budgets and the don't overachieve principle

Rather than requiring 100 percent, it is better to allow an error budget, a rate at which the SLOs can be missed, and track it on a daily or weekly basis. A key insight: users build on the reality of what you offer, rather than what you say you will supply, particularly for infrastructure services. If actual performance greatly exceeds the stated SLO, users come to depend on the higher level. In the Chubby lock service case study, dependent services assumed it would never go down, which created unsafe dependencies; Google deliberately triggered controlled outages to keep reliance in line with the published SLO. Do not overachieve: publish and defend a realistic level rather than an accidental one.

title: Google SRE Book, Chapter 3: Embracing Risk (Betsy Beyer et al.)
text:
## 100 percent is the wrong target

SRE rejects the assumption that 100 percent reliability is desirable. Past a certain point increasing reliability is worse for a service and its users rather than better, because extreme reliability constrains how fast features can ship and raises cost disproportionately, while users usually cannot perceive the difference between very high reliability levels once their own devices and networks introduce failures. The right availability target is treated as both a minimum and a maximum.

## The cost of reliability

Cost does not increase linearly as reliability increments. Each additional nine of availability can cost roughly 100 times more than the previous one. Two cost dimensions matter: direct costs of redundant equipment and resources, and the opportunity cost of engineering capacity diverted from building user facing features.

## Measuring availability

Time based availability equals uptime over total time. A 99.99 percent target permits about 52.56 minutes of downtime per year. Aggregate availability, or request success rate, equals successful requests divided by total requests over a rolling window, which suits distributed systems where partial failure is normal. A service serving 2.5 million requests per day at 99.99 percent may fail up to 250 requests that day.

## The nines

Availability is quoted in nines: 99.9 percent is three nines, 99.99 percent is four nines, 99.999 percent is five nines. Each added nine is an order of magnitude closer to perfect.

## Risk tolerance

For consumer services the target depends on user expectations, competitive positioning, revenue impact, and whether the service is free or paid. Google Apps for Work targets 99.9 percent given enterprise dependence, while early YouTube in 2006 chose a lower target to prioritize rapid feature development. Infrastructure services with many clients use explicitly delineated levels of service: Bigtable offers low latency clusters with provisioned slack for reliability alongside throughput clusters run very hot at 10 to 50 percent of the cost. A cost benefit example: moving a $1M revenue service from 99.9 to 99.99 percent (a 0.09 percent gain) yields about $900 of value, so it is only worth doing if it costs less than $900.

## Error budgets

An error budget is one minus the availability target. For a 99.999 percent SLO the error budget is 0.001 percent of requests over the period. Product Management sets the SLO, monitoring measures actual uptime, and the difference is the remaining budget for the quarter; new releases proceed as long as measured uptime is above the SLO. Error budgets remove the politics from negotiations between product and SRE by giving both sides an objective, agreed metric. When the budget is nearly spent, product teams self regulate and raise testing rigor rather than needing SRE to enforce a freeze. Loosening an SLO increases the error budget and permits faster launches, aligning both teams on finding the right balance guided by measurement rather than politics, fear, or hope.

title: Google SRE Book, Chapter 5: Eliminating Toil (Betsy Beyer et al.)
text:
## What toil is

Toil is the kind of work tied to running a production service that tends to be manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, devoid of enduring value, and that scales linearly as a service grows. Toil is not simply work you do not like to do, and it is not the same as overhead. Overhead is administrative work such as meetings, HR paperwork, or expense reports; toil is operational work that directly keeps the service running.

## Six characteristics of toil

Work qualifies as toil to the degree it is: manual, requiring hands on human time even to run a script; repetitive, done again and again rather than a one time fix; automatable, meaning a machine could do it as well as a human; tactical, interrupt driven and reactive rather than strategy driven; without enduring value, leaving the service in the same state after it is done; and scaling linearly with service growth, so headcount would have to grow with traffic.

## The 50 percent target

Google SRE aims to keep each engineer's toil below 50 percent of their time, reserving the majority for engineering project work that reduces future toil or adds service features. Surveys put the actual average near 33 percent, with individuals ranging from 0 to 80 percent. A floor of toil exists because of on call and interrupts, roughly 25 to 33 percent depending on rotation size.

## Why toil is bad

Too much toil causes career stagnation, low morale, and attrition, and it slows progress because time spent on toil is time not spent engineering. It also creates confusion about the mission: SRE is an engineering organization, and behavior that treats it as a pure operations team erodes that identity. Excess toil can also normalize an unsustainable path where the team cannot keep up as the service grows. The remedy is to spend the engineering half of time on software and systems work that permanently removes toil, so a service can scale without a matching increase in operational load.

title: Google SRE Book, Chapter 6: Monitoring Distributed Systems, the Four Golden Signals (Betsy Beyer et al.)
text:
## The Four Golden Signals

If you can measure only four metrics of your user facing system, focus on latency, traffic, errors, and saturation. Latency is the time it takes to service a request; it is important to distinguish the latency of successful requests from the latency of failed requests, because a fast error can otherwise hide in the good latency numbers. Traffic is a measure of demand on the system, for example HTTP requests per second for a web service, network I/O rate, or concurrent sessions. Errors is the rate of requests that fail, either explicitly such as HTTP 500s, implicitly such as an HTTP 200 returned with the wrong content, or by policy such as any request slower than a committed threshold. Saturation is how full the service is, a measure of the fraction of the most constrained resource; many systems degrade in performance before they hit 100 percent utilization, so a utilization target is important.

## Why monitor

Monitoring exists to analyze long term trends, to compare over time and across experiments, to alert when something is broken or about to break, to build dashboards, and to conduct retrospective debugging. Good monitoring lets a system tell you when it is broken, or better, what is about to break.

## Symptoms versus causes

A monitoring system should address what is broken, the symptom, and why, the cause. The what versus why distinction is one of the most important in writing good monitoring with maximum signal and minimum noise. A user visible symptom (the website is slow) is separated from its cause (an overloaded database). Alert on symptoms that indicate real user impact.

## Black box and white box

White box monitoring is based on metrics exposed by the internals of the system, including logs and interfaces, and can detect imminent problems and failures masked by retries. Black box monitoring is symptom oriented and tests externally visible behavior as a user would see it, representing active, ongoing problems rather than predicted ones. A robust setup combines both.

## Alerting philosophy

When writing alerting rules, keep pages meaningful: every page should be urgent, actionable, and require intelligence, not a mechanical response. Pages that can be safely ignored are worse than no page because they train responders to ignore alerts. Symptoms that reflect definite user impact are better paging triggers than causes. Humans fatigue quickly, so a page must reflect a real, ongoing problem that only a human can address.

title: Google SRE Book, Chapter 15: Postmortem Culture, Learning from Failure (Betsy Beyer et al.)
text:
## What a postmortem is

A postmortem is a written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, the root cause or causes, and the follow up actions to prevent recurrence. Incidents and outages are inevitable given the scale and velocity of change, so the goal is to institutionalize learning from them rather than to avoid ever having them.

## Blameless postmortems

A blameless postmortem focuses on identifying the contributing causes of the incident without indicting any individual or team for bad or inappropriate behavior. It assumes that everyone involved had good intentions and did the right thing with the information they had at the time. The mindset shifts from allocating blame to investigating the systematic reasons why an individual or team had incomplete or incorrect information. The core belief: you cannot fix people, but you can fix systems and processes to better support people making the right choices when designing and maintaining complex systems.

## Triggers

Common criteria that should trigger a postmortem include user visible downtime or degradation beyond a threshold, data loss of any kind, on call engineer intervention such as a rollback or diverting traffic, a resolution time above some threshold, and a monitoring failure that meant a problem was discovered by a human rather than by an alert. Teams agree these criteria in advance so postmortems are expected, not a punishment.

## Best practices

Remove blame so people have the confidence to escalate issues without fear. Do not stigmatize teams that file many postmortems; a high count reflects transparency, not incompetence. Ensure senior engineers review a postmortem before it is published, and share it broadly so the whole organization can learn. Visibly reward the people who do the work of writing effective postmortems and closing the follow up items. A postmortem that is filed but whose action items are never completed is of little value, so track the follow ups to completion.

title: Google SRE Book, Chapter 11: Being On-Call (Betsy Beyer et al.)
text:
## Balanced on-call, by quantity and quality

Google caps operational load: SREs spend at least 50 percent of their time on engineering, and across the remainder no more than 25 percent is spent on call, leaving up to 25 percent for other operational work. Balance has two dimensions: quantity, the fraction of time spent on call, and quality, how many incidents occur during a shift.

## Team sizing

Because of the 25 percent on call ceiling, a single site team running a 24/7 rotation with a primary and a secondary needs a minimum of about eight engineers, so each person covers roughly one week per month. Multi site follow the sun rotations spread load across time zones and can reduce night shifts.

## Incident load target

Properly handling an incident, including root cause analysis, remediation, and writing the postmortem, takes about 6 hours. This leads to a hard limit of a maximum of 2 incidents per 12 hour on call shift. If a rotation regularly exceeds that, the service is generating too much operational load and the fix is to push work back to engineering and to the development team, not to absorb more toil.

## Response times

Response time expectations follow from the SLO. User facing or otherwise time critical services may require a response within about 5 minutes, while less sensitive services may allow 30 minutes. A service with a four nines availability target has roughly 13 minutes of downtime budget per quarter, which constrains how fast a page must be answered.

## Primary, secondary, and psychological safety

Rotations typically have a primary on call and a secondary; some teams use the secondary as a backstop for missed pages, others route non urgent work to the secondary. Key supports for on call resilience are clear escalation paths, well defined incident management procedures, and a blameless postmortem culture. Out of hours work should be compensated with time off in lieu or cash, capped as a proportion of salary, to reward participation without encouraging burnout.

title: DORA, The Four Keys and Software Delivery Performance Metrics
text:
## The metrics of software delivery performance

DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment) measures software delivery performance with a small set of metrics that have grown from the original four keys. They divide into two groups: throughput, how quickly and how often change moves through the system, and stability or instability, how well those changes behave in production.

## Throughput metrics

Change lead time is the amount of time it takes for a change to go from committed to version control to deployed and running in production. Deployment frequency is the number of deployments over a given period, or equivalently the time between deployments. Failed deployment recovery time is the time it takes to recover from a deployment that fails and requires immediate intervention; this metric replaced the earlier time to restore service framing as the model matured.

## Stability metrics

Change fail rate is the ratio of deployments that require immediate intervention (such as a hotfix, rollback, patch, or roll forward) following the deployment. Deployment rework rate, a newer signal, is the ratio of deployments that are unplanned and happen as a result of an incident in production.

## Why these metrics

Throughput and stability are not a tradeoff. The DORA research repeatedly finds that the highest performing teams do well on both at once: they ship small changes frequently with short lead times and also have low change failure rates and recover fast. Chasing speed by cutting quality, or chasing stability by slowing down, both tend to make the other worse. The four keys are outcome metrics: they are meant to be watched as a system and improved by investing in the underlying technical and cultural capabilities, not gamed individually.

title: Adam Wiggins (Heroku), The Twelve-Factor App
text:
## What the twelve-factor app is

The twelve-factor app is a methodology for building software as a service apps that use declarative formats for setup automation to minimize time and cost for new developers, have a clean contract with the underlying operating system for maximum portability, are suitable for deployment on modern cloud platforms, minimize divergence between development and production to enable continuous deployment, and can scale up without significant changes to tooling, architecture, or development practices. It is language and backing service agnostic.

## The twelve factors

I. Codebase: one codebase tracked in revision control, many deploys. II. Dependencies: explicitly declare and isolate dependencies, never relying on implicit system wide packages. III. Config: store config in the environment, strictly separated from code, so the same build can run in any environment. IV. Backing services: treat backing services such as databases, queues, and SMTP as attached resources reachable by a URL or locator in config, swappable without code changes. V. Build, release, run: strictly separate the build stage, the release stage that combines build with config, and the run stage; releases are immutable and can be rolled back. VI. Processes: execute the app as one or more stateless, share nothing processes; persistent data belongs in a stateful backing service. VII. Port binding: export services via port binding, the app is self contained and does not rely on runtime injection of a webserver. VIII. Concurrency: scale out via the process model, handling different workloads with different process types. IX. Disposability: maximize robustness with fast startup and graceful shutdown, so processes can be started or stopped at a moment's notice. X. Dev/prod parity: keep development, staging, and production as similar as possible, closing the time, personnel, and tools gaps to enable continuous deployment. XI. Logs: treat logs as event streams written unbuffered to stdout, leaving routing and storage to the execution environment. XII. Admin processes: run admin and management tasks such as migrations as one off processes in an identical environment to the long running processes.

title: Principles of Chaos Engineering
text:
## Definition

Chaos Engineering is the discipline of experimenting on a system in order to build confidence in the system's capability to withstand turbulent conditions in production. Distributed systems have inherent chaos: even when each individual service works correctly, the interactions between services can produce unpredictable outcomes, compounded by rare events such as hardware faults, unreliable networks, and traffic spikes. Systemic weaknesses like improper fallback settings, retry storms from misconfigured timeouts, outages of a downstream dependency, cascading failures, and bottlenecks must be found before they affect real customers.

## The experimental method

Chaos Engineering is empirical, following the scientific method. First, define the steady state as a measurable output of the system that indicates normal behavior, such as throughput, error rate, or latency percentiles, rather than internal attributes. Second, hypothesize that this steady state will continue in both a control group and an experimental group. Third, introduce variables that reflect real world events into the experimental group. Fourth, try to disprove the hypothesis by looking for a difference in steady state between the control and experimental groups. The harder it is to disrupt the steady state, the more confidence you have in the system; a weakness found is a target for improvement before it manifests system wide.

## The advanced principles

Build a Hypothesis around Steady State Behavior: focus on the measurable output of a system, not internal attributes, and use that as a proxy for normal operation. Vary Real world Events: chaos variables should reflect real world events, prioritized by potential impact or estimated frequency, including both failures such as servers dying and non failure events such as a spike in traffic. Run Experiments in Production: to guarantee authenticity of how the system is exercised and relevance to the current deployed environment, Chaos strongly prefers to experiment directly on production traffic. Automate Experiments to Run Continuously: running experiments manually is labor intensive and unsustainable, so automate them to run continuously and catch regressions. Minimize Blast Radius: experimenting in production can cause real customer pain, so it is the engineer's responsibility to ensure the fallout is contained and minimized, building the smallest possible experiment that still teaches you something.

title: Martin Fowler, Continuous Integration
text:
## Definition

Continuous Integration is a software development practice where members of a team integrate their work frequently, usually each person integrates at least daily, leading to multiple integrations per day. Each integration is verified by an automated build, including test, to detect integration errors as quickly as possible. Teams find that this approach leads to significantly reduced integration problems and allows a team to develop cohesive software more rapidly.

## Key practices

Maintain a single source repository and put everything needed for a build into it: source, tests, database schema, and build scripts, so anyone can check out onto a clean machine and build. Automate the build so a single command can build the system from source. Make the build self testing by including an automated test suite that can catch a large class of bugs. Everyone commits to the mainline every day, which surfaces conflicts while they are small. Every commit should build the mainline on an integration machine, using a continuous integration server that watches the repository. Keep the build fast, with a commit build targeted at around ten minutes, so feedback is rapid. Test in a clone of the production environment to catch environment specific problems. Make it easy for anyone to get the latest executable. Everyone can see what is happening through a visible build status. Automate deployment so moving a build between environments is scripted.

## Fixing broken builds

When the mainline build breaks, fixing it is the top priority of the whole team. A broken build is not a catastrophe but it should be rare, and the fastest way back to green is often to revert the last commit and diagnose on a developer machine.

## Benefits

Continuous Integration reduces integration risk: instead of a long, unpredictable, painful integration phase at the end, integrations are frequent, small, and routine. Integration effort scales non linearly, so many small integrations are far cheaper in total than a few big ones. A healthy mainline stays deployable, which makes releasing to production a business decision rather than a technical scramble, and the safety of frequent integration makes aggressive refactoring practical.

title: Martin Fowler, SnowflakeServer (anti-pattern)
text:
## The anti-pattern

A SnowflakeServer is a server whose configuration is unique, built and tuned by hand over time, so that it cannot be easily reproduced. Like a snowflake, each one is delicate and unique. Snowflakes grow when administrators make manual changes directly on a running server rather than through automated, version controlled configuration.

## Why snowflakes are bad

A snowflake is hard to reproduce, which matters when hardware fails or you need to spin up another identical server to support the same function or to run a realistic test environment. Configuration drift sets in: upgrades of one piece of software cause unpredictable knock on effects, and over time nobody is sure which parts of the configuration are essential and which are cruft. The server becomes hard to understand and modify, so changes turn into long, stressful bouts of debugging. Organizations become so afraid of touching a fragile snowflake that they keep running critical software on ancient, unpatched operating systems simply because rebuilding is too risky. The deep problem is that a manually built system cannot be confidently rebuilt, so disaster recovery and horizontal scaling are both compromised.

## The remedy

Replace hand tuning with automated configuration recipes using tools such as Puppet or Chef, stored in version control so every configuration and change is recorded and auditable. Rebuild servers regularly from that automation, the PhoenixServer pattern, so the build process itself is exercised and trusted. Prefer fully automated deployments and, where possible, immutable infrastructure so a server is a disposable, reproducible artifact rather than a unique pet requiring special care. This also gives you genuinely production like test environments and fewer configuration related bugs.

title: Martin Fowler, InfrastructureAsCode
text:
## Definition

Infrastructure as Code is the approach to defining computing and network infrastructure through source code that can then be treated just like any software system. Such code is kept in a source control system, can be built and tested with the usual continuous integration and delivery tooling, and is deployed through repeatable pipelines. This makes changes to infrastructure routine and safe rather than exceptional and risky.

## Core practices

Use definition files: all configuration is captured in executable files such as shell scripts, Ansible playbooks, Chef recipes, or Puppet manifests rather than performed by hand, which prevents inconsistent snowflake systems. Self documented systems and processes: the code itself is a precise and consistent description of how the infrastructure is built, more reliable than a wiki page a human follows. Version everything: keep all this code in source control so every configuration and every change is recorded for audit. Continuously test systems and processes: automated tests catch configuration errors quickly and enable a deployment pipeline for infrastructure. Small changes rather than big batches: smaller updates are easier to test, debug, and revert than large ones. Keep services available continuously: techniques such as blue green deployment and parallel change let you update infrastructure without downtime.

## Idempotence and declarative style

A good infrastructure as code tool is idempotent, meaning applying the same definition repeatedly converges the system to the same desired state regardless of its starting point, so a run that is interrupted or repeated is safe. Declarative tools let you state the desired end state and let the tool work out the steps, which contrasts with imperative scripts that spell out each command; declarative definitions are generally easier to reason about and to keep idempotent.

## Benefits

Infrastructure as Code brings consistency across servers, makes changes safer through faster fault detection and recovery, improves compliance because every change is auditable and version controlled, and scales to managing large clusters of servers, which is essential for practices like microservices and dynamic cloud provisioning.

title: Martin Fowler, BlueGreenDeployment
text:
## Definition

Blue green deployment is a release technique that reduces downtime and risk by running two production environments as identical as possible, called blue and green. At any time only one of them, say blue, is live and serving all production traffic while the other, green, is idle.

## How the switch works

When you prepare a new release you deploy it to the idle environment, green, and do your final testing there. When green is ready, you switch the router or load balancer so that all incoming requests go to green; blue is now idle. Green is live, and blue is your last known good version standing by. Because the cutover is just a routing change, it can happen with little or no downtime.

## Rollback

Rollback is fast and simple: if anything goes wrong on the newly live environment you switch the router back to blue, restoring the previous version almost instantly. Because blue is kept intact, you always have an immediate escape hatch, and each release also exercises your ability to fail over, which keeps disaster recovery procedures honest.

## The database challenge

The hard part is stateful backing services, especially the database, which is shared or must be migrated. The recommended approach is to decouple schema changes from code changes: first apply schema changes that are backward and forward compatible so both the old and new application versions can run against them, verify that as a safe rollback point, then deploy the new application code. Keeping migrations compatible with both versions is what makes the instantaneous switch and rollback possible without data loss.

title: Danilo Sato (martinfowler.com), CanaryRelease
text:
## Definition

Canary release is a technique to reduce the risk of introducing a new software version in production by slowly rolling out the change to a small subset of users before rolling it out to the entire infrastructure and making it available to everybody. The name comes from the canary in a coal mine: the small early exposure gives you a warning before harm spreads.

## How it works

You deploy the new version alongside the current stable version but route no user to it at first. Then you start routing a few selected users to the new version, watching key metrics closely. As confidence grows you increase the number of servers running the new version and the amount of traffic sent to it, until eventually all traffic and all infrastructure are on the new version and the old one is retired. Because production capacity is being exercised for real, you get a truthful signal that a separate staging environment cannot give.

## Choosing who gets the canary

Strategies for selecting the subset include random sampling of users, exposing internal or employee users first, or targeting a specific demographic or region so the blast radius is understood.

## Rollback and risk

If the monitored business and system metrics regress, rollback is simple: route traffic back to the old version. This makes canary a low risk way to test in production. It differs from A/B testing: a canary detects regressions and problems by monitoring, while A/B testing measures which of two variants performs better on a business hypothesis. Mixing the two concerns can compromise the results, and A/B tests typically need days for statistical significance whereas a canary can complete in minutes or hours. Operational challenges include running multiple versions at once, backward compatible database schema changes, and, for software on user devices, limited control over upgrades.

title: DORA, Research Program and State of DevOps
text:
## The research program

DORA runs one of the longest running, academically rigorous research investigations of its kind, using behavioral science to connect ways of working, through software delivery performance, to organizational goals and individual well being. The findings are published in the annual Accelerate State of DevOps reports and distilled into the DORA Core Model of capabilities, metrics, and outcomes, which deliberately trails the research and evolves conservatively so practitioners can rely on it.

## The central finding

Software delivery performance, measured by the throughput and stability metrics (the four keys), is a statistically significant predictor of organizational performance, including profitability, productivity, market share, and non commercial goals, as well as of team well being and reduced burnout. Speed and stability go together rather than trading off; elite performers do well on both.

## Capabilities that drive performance

The research identifies technical, process, and cultural capabilities that causally improve the four keys. Technical capabilities include version control for everything, continuous integration, trunk based development, deployment automation, test automation, continuous testing, loosely coupled architecture, and continuous delivery. Process and measurement capabilities include working in small batches, monitoring and observability, and proactive notification. Cultural capabilities include a generative, high trust culture (Westrum), psychological safety, learning culture, and transformational leadership.

## Performance clusters and later findings

The reports cluster teams into performance groups, with the Elite cluster representing the highest level of software delivery performance, above High, Medium, and Low. Later years added nuance: high quality internal documentation is foundational and amplifies technical capabilities, user centricity predicts markedly higher performance, security is cultural rather than purely technical, and in 2025 the message on AI is that it acts as an amplifier while the greatest returns still come from improving the underlying sociotechnical system, not the tool alone.

title: Google SRE Book, Chapter 8: Release Engineering (Betsy Beyer et al.)
text:
## What release engineering is

Release engineering is a distinct discipline focused on building and delivering software: taking source code and configuration and turning it into a running production service in a reproducible, automated way so that releases are repeatable. Release engineers are fluent in source control, compilers, build tools, package managers, and installers, and they work at the intersection of development, configuration management, testing, and operations, defining every step from the source repository to the deployed binary.

## Four guiding principles

Self service model: to scale, teams must run their own releases, so release engineering builds tools and best practices that let each product team control its own release frequency and cadence with minimal manual involvement. High velocity: releasing frequently means fewer changes between versions, which makes testing and troubleshooting easier; some teams build hourly or adopt Push on Green, deploying every build that passes its tests. Hermetic builds: a build must be hermetic, meaning it gives identical results regardless of the machine it runs on and is insensitive to the libraries and other software installed on the build host; it depends only on known, versioned tools and dependencies checked into source control, so rebuilding an old release six months later produces the same artifact. Enforcement of policies and procedures: gates such as code review, approvals for who may perform each operation, and controls on who can deploy are enforced by tooling, not left to trust.

## Continuous build, deployment, and configuration

Google's automated Rapid system builds, tests, packages, and deploys at scale through defined workflows that run serially or in parallel. Configuration is managed deliberately: it may live on the mainline with the code, be packaged with the binary, ship as a separate configuration package, or be read from an external store, with the choice driven by how independently config and code need to change. The overarching aim is that both binaries and their configuration are produced by an automated, versioned, reproducible pipeline rather than assembled by hand.

title: OpenTelemetry, Observability Primer
text:
## Observability

Observability is the ability to understand the internal state of a system by examining its outputs, so you can ask arbitrary new questions about the system and answer why something is happening without shipping new code. A system is observable only if it is properly instrumented: the application code must emit signals such as traces, metrics, and logs. When an application is well instrumented, developers do not need to add more instrumentation to troubleshoot an issue because they already have the information they need.

## Telemetry and instrumentation

Telemetry is the data emitted from a system about its behavior, delivered as signals. Instrumentation is the code that makes a system emit that telemetry.

## The three signals: logs, metrics, traces

A log is a timestamped message emitted by a service or component, not necessarily tied to any particular request; logs are useful but on their own lack request context. A metric is an aggregation over a period of time of numeric data about your infrastructure or application, for example error rate, request count, or CPU utilization, good for dashboards and alerting. A trace records the path of a single request as it propagates through the services of a distributed system, giving the request level context that logs and metrics alone lack.

## Spans and distributed tracing

A span represents a single unit of work or operation and carries a name, timing data, and structured metadata called attributes; spans have parent child relationships. A distributed trace, often just called a trace, records the paths taken by a request as it moves through a multi service architecture, and is made up of one or more spans, commonly visualized as a waterfall. Together, correlated traces, metrics, and logs are what make a modern distributed system observable.

## Reliability, SLIs, and SLOs

Reliability is whether a service does what its users expect it to do, measured from the user's point of view rather than from raw uptime. A Service Level Indicator (SLI) measures a specific dimension of that behavior, and a Service Level Objective (SLO) sets a target for an SLI and communicates the intended reliability across the organization by tying it to business value.

title: Google SRE Workbook, Chapter 5: Alerting on SLOs (burn rate)
text:
## Why naive threshold alerting fails

Alerting simply when the error rate crosses the SLO threshold produces terrible signal. With a 99.9 percent SLO and a short 10 minute evaluation window, you could receive up to 144 alerts per day, act on none of them, and still meet the SLO for the month. Short fixed windows have poor precision (they fire on brief, harmless blips) and long fixed windows have poor reset time (they keep firing long after the problem is over). This constant, low value paging is the root of alert fatigue.

## Error budget burn rate

The better approach alerts on how fast you are consuming the error budget, called the burn rate. Burn rate is defined relative to the SLO window: a burn rate of 1 means you are spending the entire budget exactly over the SLO period, for a 99.9 percent monthly SLO that is a sustained 0.1 percent error rate over 30 days. A burn rate of 10 (a sustained 1 percent error rate) exhausts a 30 day budget in about 3 days. Higher burn rate means faster exhaustion and more urgency.

## Multiwindow, multi burn rate alerts

The recommended pattern combines several burn rate alerts, each defined as a fraction of the budget consumed over a window, and each additionally gated by a shorter window so it only fires while errors are actively happening: a fast page at a burn rate of 14.4 over a 1 hour window (plus a 5 minute short window) fires when about 2 percent of the 30 day budget is consumed; a slower page at a burn rate of 6 over a 6 hour window (plus a 30 minute short window) fires at about 5 percent of the budget; and a ticket, not a page, at a burn rate of 1 over a 3 day window (plus a 6 hour short window) fires at about 10 percent of the budget. This gives good precision and good recall, pages only on genuinely fast burns, and files a low urgency ticket for slow burns, dramatically cutting false pages while still catching real threats early.

title: Gene Kim (IT Revolution), The Three Ways: The Principles Underpinning DevOps
text:
## The Three Ways

Gene Kim describes three principles, the Three Ways, from which all the observed DevOps patterns can be derived. They are the philosophical foundation for The Phoenix Project and The DevOps Handbook.

## The First Way: flow and systems thinking

The First Way emphasizes the performance of the entire system, the whole value stream from Development through IT Operations to the customer, as opposed to the performance of a specific silo, department, or individual. The outcomes of the First Way include never passing a known defect downstream, never allowing local optimization to cause global degradation, always seeking to increase flow, and achieving a deep understanding of the system. Practices that follow include small batch sizes, reducing work in process, and building quality in at the source.

## The Second Way: amplify feedback loops

The Second Way is about creating right to left feedback loops. The goal of almost any process improvement is to shorten and amplify feedback loops so that necessary corrections can be made continually. The outcomes include understanding and responding to all customers internal and external, shortening and amplifying feedback, and embedding knowledge where it is needed. Fast feedback stops problems from recurring and lets you detect and recover faster.

## The Third Way: culture of continual experimentation and learning

The Third Way is about creating a culture that fosters two things at once: continual experimentation, taking risks and learning from success and failure, and understanding that repetition and practice are the prerequisite to mastery. This Way calls for allocating time to improve daily work, rewarding teams for taking risks, and deliberately introducing faults into the system to increase resilience. The push and pull of these two forces is what continually improves the operation of the system and creates safety alongside high velocity.

title: Kief Morris (martinfowler.com), ImmutableServer
text:
## Definition

An immutable server is a server that, once deployed, is never modified in place; it is merely replaced with a new, updated instance. Instead of logging in to change a running server, you change the base image or definition, test it, and deploy fresh instances built from that validated image, then destroy the old ones.

## Relationship to Phoenix and Snowflake servers

The immutable server builds on the PhoenixServer idea, a server that can be torn down and rebuilt at will from a base image, which eliminates the configuration drift that accumulates on long lived systems. It is the opposite of the SnowflakeServer, the fragile, hand tuned, hard to reproduce system that the pattern is designed to abolish.

## The core rule

Once an instance is launched from a tested base image you should not run configuration management tools against it, because doing so opens the door to untested changes on that specific instance. Configuration management moves earlier: changes are made to the image first, not to running servers. Any legitimate per instance variation should come from external sources such as provisioning metadata or a central registry, not from post deployment edits.

## Benefits

The approach mirrors continuous delivery: just as a compiled artifact is built once and promoted unchanged across environments, an immutable instance built from a given image is identical everywhere it runs. This removes configuration drift, makes rollback trivial (destroy the new instances and redeploy the previous image), and guarantees reproducibility, which is why it pairs naturally with automated image baking and infrastructure as code.

title: OpenGitOps (CNCF), GitOps Principles v1.0.0
text:
## What GitOps is

OpenGitOps is a set of open source standards, best practices, and community focused education, hosted in the CNCF, to help organizations adopt a structured, standardized approach to implementing GitOps. GitOps is a set of principles for operating and managing software systems in which the desired state of the whole system is described declaratively and stored in a version controlled source of truth (typically Git), and automated agents make the running system match that stored desired state.

## The four GitOps principles

1. Declarative: a system managed by GitOps must have its desired state expressed declaratively, describing what the system should look like rather than the imperative steps to get there. 2. Versioned and Immutable: desired state is stored in a way that enforces immutability and versioning and retains a complete version history, so any past state can be recovered and every change is auditable. 3. Pulled Automatically: software agents automatically pull the desired state declarations from the source, rather than having changes pushed into the cluster by a CI pipeline with standing credentials. 4. Continuously Reconciled: software agents continuously observe the actual system state and attempt to apply the desired state, so drift is detected and corrected automatically and the source of truth stays authoritative.

## Why it matters

Because the whole system state lives in version control and is continuously reconciled, GitOps gives you auditable change history, easy rollback by reverting a commit, drift detection, and a consistent workflow (a pull request) for changing production, which pairs naturally with infrastructure as code and immutable infrastructure.

title: AWS Well-Architected Framework, Reliability Pillar Design Principles
text:
## Reliability design principles

The AWS Well-Architected Framework Reliability Pillar lists design principles that increase reliability in the cloud.

Automatically recover from failure: monitor a workload for key performance indicators (KPIs) that measure business value, not just technical operation, and run automation when a threshold is breached, enabling automatic notification, tracking, and recovery processes that work around or repair the failure; with more sophisticated automation you can anticipate and remediate failures before they occur.

Test recovery procedures: unlike on premises testing that only proves a workload works in a given scenario, in the cloud you can test how your workload fails and validate your recovery procedures, using automation to simulate different failures or recreate past failure scenarios, exposing failure pathways you can test and fix before a real failure occurs and thereby reducing risk. This is the cloud embodiment of chaos engineering and game days.

Scale horizontally to increase aggregate workload availability: replace one large resource with multiple small resources and distribute requests across them so no single failure takes down the whole workload and there is no shared common point of failure.

Stop guessing capacity: a common cause of on premises failure is resource saturation, when demand exceeds capacity; in the cloud you monitor demand and utilization and automate adding or removing resources to match demand without over or under provisioning.

Manage change in automation: changes to infrastructure should be made using automation, and the changes that must be managed include changes to the automation itself, so that every change is tracked and reviewed rather than made by hand.

title: Martin Fowler, MonolithFirst (anti-pattern for microservices-first)
text:
## The argument

MonolithFirst is the observation that teams building a new application should almost always start with a monolith, even if they expect microservices later. Fowler's empirical point: almost all the successful microservice stories started with a monolith that got too big and was broken up, while most systems built as microservices from scratch ran into serious trouble. Jumping straight to microservices is a common and costly anti-pattern.

## The microservice premium

Microservices carry a premium: the added complexity of managing many services, network calls, distributed data, and operational tooling. That premium only pays off for systems complex enough to need it. Early on, when you most need to iterate fast and get feedback, the premium slows you down for little benefit.

## Why boundaries are the problem

The hardest part of microservices is drawing the right service boundaries, the bounded contexts, and you rarely know them at the start of a project. Refactoring functionality between services is much harder than moving it within a monolith, so premature decomposition locks in boundaries that turn out to be wrong and are expensive to change. Starting with a monolith (ideally a well modularized one) lets you learn the domain and discover natural seams before you pay to split them.

## How to proceed

Practical strategies include designing a modular monolith and separating modules into services only as they prove they need it, gradually peeling services off the edges of the monolith, and treating an initial monolith as a sacrificial architecture you expect to replace. Going microservices first can be justified when the team already has deep microservices experience or is replacing a system whose boundaries are already well understood, but for a genuinely new product, monolith first is the lower risk default.

title: DX, DORA Metrics Benchmarks (Elite/High/Medium/Low thresholds)
text:
## DORA performance benchmark thresholds

DORA research groups teams into four performance levels, Elite, High, Medium, and Low, by their scores on the four keys. A widely cited benchmark table maps each metric to each level.

Elite performers: deployment frequency of multiple deploys per day (on demand); lead time for changes of less than one day; change failure rate of 0 to 15 percent; and time to restore service of less than one hour.

High performers: deployment frequency of between once per day and once per week; lead time for changes of one day to one week; change failure rate of 16 to 30 percent; and time to restore service of less than one day.

Medium performers: deployment frequency of between once per week and once per month; lead time for changes of one week to one month; change failure rate of 16 to 30 percent; and time to restore service of one day to one week.

Low performers: deployment frequency of between once per month and once every six months; lead time for changes of one to six months; change failure rate of 46 to 60 percent; and time to restore service of one week to one month.

## The key interpretation

High performance combines high throughput and low instability, and neither should be traded for the other: the exact thresholds shift from year to year as the industry improves, so treat the levels as a relative benchmark and a direction of travel, not a fixed finish line. Note the exact cutoffs vary between DORA report years, so cite the specific report year when quoting a threshold precisely.
